plan.title: Fish Can Fly
plan.outro: Salmon in the river, DNA in the air.

beats.narration: Salmon are swimming up a river,
and somewhere above the water, a passive air sampler sits,
collecting whatever drifts past. Can that air tell you which fish are there?
This repository holds the full study that asks exactly that:
passive air sampling detects environmental DNA transfer from water into air.

elements.text: detects environmental DNA transfer from *water* into *air*.

beats.narration: It is for anyone who wants to check the claim, or reuse the approach.
You open one R project, nicknamed Fish can fly,
run the scripts,
and the figures from the paper come back out.
Everything sits beside it: the raw field and lab data, the model outputs,
the figures, the final manuscript, and the peer review comments.
So the path starts with raw data, left untouched.
There are qPCR runs from air samples for coho and chinook,
salmon standards, and fish counts for both species,
plus weather records.
The R scripts load and clean them,
then hand them to a single Stan joint model.
That model returns posterior distributions, saved to the output folder,
and the plotting routines turn those into every figure.
But why one joint model?
Because the counts, the qPCR standards and the air signal are fitted together,
so uncertainty in each flows into the others.
Which means the answer to the opening question comes with error bars...
fish counted in the river, measured in the air.
